title: The Cellar of Harrow Glen
premise: Paloma Ravensworth, a pest controller with a talent for being overlooked, is hired to investigate sounds in the cellar of Harrow Glen, a decaying house where the Aldous family has quietly been unraveling for years. The noises have fingerprints—small, deliberate, almost affectionate—and when Paloma's overnight audio recordings capture a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud, he realizes something in the cellar has been counting the family members, and the count is nearly complete. Falling for Wren Aldous while concealing what he knows, Paloma must choose between his lifelong instinct to stay invisible and the duty of pulling the family out before the final tally. In the end, he offers the thing below a trade: himself as the last name on its list, buying the family's escape—but surviving it only by letting the cellar learn his true name, an act that erases who he was and leaves him remembered by no one except Wren.
about_author: Juniper Quintana is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade crawling through other people's basements and swears half of them were listening back. They write horror about houses that keep records and the people too polite to ask what for.

chapters.title: The Call Comes at Dusk
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Paloma, who takes the Harrow Glen job because it pays triple and because the caller knew his unlisted number. He arrives to find the Aldouses oddly calm, as if they've been waiting for someone to confirm what they refuse to say. Emotional beat: unease dressed up as professionalism.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Flour
chapters.summary: Paloma inspects the cellar and finds small handprints pressed into dust, flour, even condensation—always five fingers, always slightly too long. POV: Paloma. He logs them as rodent-adjacent anomalies, lying to his own report. Beat: the first crack in his rationalist armor.

chapters.title: The Family That Doesn't Look Up
chapters.summary: Wren Aldous's POV. She introduces the household: her fading mother, her silent brother Tam, her father who hasn't left the house in four years. She notices Paloma noticing things, and for the first time feels seen herself. Beat: cautious connection amid dread.

chapters.title: Three Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Paloma's POV: the noises began three years ago in his own flat, and he built a career out of explaining them away for other people. He tells himself Harrow Glen is just another job. Beat: denial revealed as survival strategy.

chapters.title: Recording Night One
chapters.summary: Paloma sets recorders in the cellar and stays awake listening. At 3:11 a.m., a voice asks, 'Is the counter still coming?' and a second voice answers. POV: Paloma. Beat: terror sharpened into obsession—he replays the tape until dawn.

chapters.title: Wren's Ledger
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She shows Paloma her grandmother's ledger, a list of names with dates, each crossed out on the day they 'moved away.' The last uncrossed entries are her mother, Tam, her father—and a blank line. Beat: love and duty beginning to pull against each other.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Paloma cross-references the ledger with parish records: everyone on the list died inside the house, and each death followed a night of recorded voices. The blank line isn't empty—it's waiting. POV: Paloma. Beat: cold clarity; the horror becomes arithmetic.

chapters.title: Tam Speaks Backwards
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Her brother begins answering questions before they're asked, in reversed syllables, and the cellar door stands open each morning though it was locked. The family's numbness is revealed as protection: they stopped looking up so it would stop counting. Beat: grief disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Getting Them Out Is Not That Simple
chapters.summary: Paloma tries to convince the Aldouses to leave; their mother calmly explains that leaving early means it follows, and following means it never stops counting. POV: Paloma. Beat: frustration curdling into helplessness—the rules are worse than the monster.

chapters.title: The Voice Uses His Name
chapters.summary: Night recordings now include Paloma's own name, spoken gently, like an invitation. He realizes staying invisible—his lifelong talent—is failing; the house has decided he exists. POV: Paloma. Beat: identity under siege.

chapters.title: What Wren Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She recalls a sister no one else remembers, whose name appears crossed out in the ledger in handwriting that matches her own. Memory itself is unreliable in Harrow Glen; the house edits. Beat: intimate horror—doubting your own past.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Was Never There
chapters.summary: Paloma interviews a former neighbor who insists she lived next door for decades, yet every record says the lot has been vacant since 1971. She hums the same tune as the recordings. POV: Paloma. Beat: widening dread beyond the house's walls.

chapters.title: A Night Above the Cellar Door
chapters.summary: Paloma and Wren keep vigil together over the locked cellar door, sharing stories to stay awake—her childhood, his invented one. Something knocks politely, twice, then waits. Beat: tenderness blooming in terror; the love story crystallizes.

chapters.title: The Rules of the Count
chapters.summary: Through Tam's backwards speech and the ledger, the rules emerge: the entity counts those who acknowledge it; acknowledgment can be given or taken; a name freely offered can substitute for a name owed. POV: Paloma. Beat: hope with a terrible price attached.

chapters.title: Mother Crosses Herself Out
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Their mother walks down to the cellar voluntarily, saying she's tired of being counted, and by morning her ledger line is struck through and no one but Wren remembers her face clearly. Beat: devastating loss and proof the substitution works.

chapters.title: Paloma's Real Name
chapters.summary: Paloma confesses to Wren that 'Ravensworth' is invented—a name he chose to disappear behind after his own family stopped counting him. To offer himself, he must give the cellar his true name, the one he buried. Beat: identity theme made literal; vulnerability as sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Last Night of Harrow Glen
chapters.summary: The family packs while the house fights back—doors relocating, stairs lengthening, the recordings playing everyone's voices at once. POV alternates between Paloma and Wren. Beat: frantic, claustrophobic escape sequence toward the climax.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Climax part one: the front door opens onto the cellar stair. Paloma realizes the only way out is down. He speaks his true name aloud at the threshold, and the counting stops mid-number. POV: Paloma. Beat: sacrificial resolve.

chapters.title: The Bargain Below
chapters.summary: Climax part two: in the cellar, the entity—revealed as a congregation of all the counted, wearing their fingerprints—accepts Paloma's offered name in exchange for the family's freedom. Wren refuses to leave without him; he lies to her, gently, one last time. Beat: love against duty, fully collided.

chapters.title: Morning, Empty House
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The Aldouses walk out into daylight; the house behind them is simply a house. Wren carries the ledger and one memory the house couldn't edit: Paloma's face. Beat: grief and gratitude entwined.

chapters.title: The Man With No Name
chapters.summary: Epilogue-style chapter from Paloma's fractured POV: he exists in the cellar's keeping, nameless, watching the family through the flour-dusted prints. But Wren, outside, whispers his chosen name every night—and somewhere below, something answers to it. Beat: bittersweet persistence of identity through love.

chapters.title: Harrow Glen, Revisited
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Wren's POV, one year later. She buys the house, moves in, and sets a recorder in the cellar. At 3:11 a.m., a familiar voice answers her questions. She crosses nothing out; instead she writes new names in the ledger—beginning a count of her own. Beat: resolution as reclamation; the horror domesticated into devotion.
